stem: At 2 a.m. an actively exploited flaw must be patched on a public server before the weekly CAB meets. What is the BEST way to proceed?

options.text: Use the emergency change process (ECAB/emergency approver), apply the fix with a rollback plan, and document with a post-implementation review
options.rationale: Emergency change expedites approval for urgent fixes while preserving rollback readiness and after-the-fact documentation and review.

options.text: Apply the patch and skip all documentation since it is an emergency
options.rationale: Emergency status expedites approval but never authorizes skipping documentation or the post-implementation review.

options.text: Wait for the regular weekly CAB regardless of active exploitation
options.rationale: Waiting leaves an actively exploited public server exposed; that is why the emergency path exists.

options.text: Let any engineer change production without any approval
options.rationale: Unapproved 'cowboy' changes bypass control entirely; emergencies still require expedited authorization.

stem: What is the purpose of a Request for Change (RFC)?

options.text: To formally document a proposed change's justification, scope, risk, implementation, and rollback plan
options.rationale: The RFC initiates the change process by capturing the reason, scope, risk, and rollback plan for review.

options.text: To permanently disable change tracking
options.rationale: An RFC enables controlled change, not the disabling of tracking.

options.text: To assign blame after an outage
options.rationale: An RFC is a forward-looking change proposal, not a blame-assignment tool.

options.text: To purchase new hardware without approval
options.rationale: An RFC documents a change for approval; it is not a bypass for procurement.

stem: Before a change is approved for implementation, which element must be confirmed to exist FIRST for the change to be considered ready?

options.text: A documented rollback (back-out) plan to restore the prior known-good state
options.rationale: A change is not ready without a defined way to revert if it fails; the rollback plan must exist before implementation.

options.text: A press release announcing the change
options.rationale: Public announcements are not a readiness prerequisite for a change.

options.text: A guarantee the change will never fail
options.rationale: No change can be guaranteed never to fail; that is why a rollback plan is required.

options.text: Approval to skip testing
options.rationale: Skipping testing is not a readiness criterion; a rollback plan is.

stem: A team asks the Change Advisory Board (CAB) to perform the technical work of deploying a change. Why is this request misguided?

options.text: The CAB reviews and approves or rejects changes; it does not implement them
options.rationale: The CAB is a governance body assessing risk and scheduling; execution is performed by the implementers, not the board.

options.text: The CAB is required to implement every change personally
options.rationale: This misstates the CAB's role; it governs rather than executes changes.

options.text: The CAB only handles hardware purchases
options.rationale: The CAB governs changes broadly, not just purchases, but it still does not implement them.

options.text: The CAB writes all application code
options.rationale: The CAB is not a development team; it reviews and approves changes.

stem: A low-risk, repeatable task like routine account provisioning follows an established, pre-approved procedure without per-instance CAB review. This is BEST described as which kind of change?

options.text: A standard (pre-approved) change
options.rationale: Standard changes are low-risk, repeatable, and pre-authorized via an established procedure, avoiding per-instance CAB review.

options.text: An emergency change
options.rationale: Emergency changes address urgent incidents; routine provisioning is not an emergency.

options.text: An unapproved ad-hoc change
options.rationale: A standard change is approved in advance via procedure, unlike an unapproved ad-hoc change.

options.text: A normal change requiring full CAB review
options.rationale: The whole point of a standard change is that it does not require full per-instance CAB review.

stem: What is the PRIMARY purpose of a post-implementation review (PIR) after a change?

options.text: To confirm the change achieved its goal, caused no adverse effects, and to capture lessons learned
options.rationale: The PIR validates outcomes and feeds improvements back into the process.

options.text: To immediately reverse every change made
options.rationale: A PIR reviews results; it does not automatically reverse successful changes.

options.text: To hide the change from auditors
options.rationale: A PIR is a documented review supporting accountability, not concealment.

options.text: To skip documentation entirely
options.rationale: The PIR is itself part of documentation, not a way to avoid it.

stem: Which statement BEST distinguishes change management from configuration management?

options.text: Change management governs how modifications are approved; configuration management maintains the authoritative baseline of deployed state
options.rationale: The two are complementary but distinct: one controls the change process, the other maintains the record of what is deployed.

options.text: They are the same process under two names
options.rationale: They are related but distinct; conflating them is a common trap.

options.text: Change management only tracks hardware inventory
options.rationale: That inventory role belongs to configuration management, not change management.

options.text: Configuration management approves emergency changes
options.rationale: Approving changes is the change-management/CAB function, not configuration management.

stem: An engineer pushes an undocumented configuration change straight to production without approval, and an outage follows. This MOST clearly demonstrates the value of what?

options.text: A formal change management process with approval, documentation, and rollback
options.rationale: Uncontrolled ad-hoc changes are a leading cause of outages; change management provides the control that prevents them.

options.text: Removing all approval steps to move faster
options.rationale: Removing approvals worsens the very problem that caused the outage.

options.text: Allowing anyone to change production at will
options.rationale: Unrestricted production changes are exactly the risk the scenario illustrates.

options.text: Deleting logs after changes
options.rationale: Deleting logs removes accountability and does not address uncontrolled change.

stem: Why are changes typically scheduled within a defined maintenance window?

options.text: To minimize disruption to business operations during the change
options.rationale: A maintenance window is an agreed low-impact period chosen to reduce operational disruption from the change.

options.text: To ensure the maximum number of users are affected
options.rationale: The goal is the opposite: minimizing user impact.

options.text: To avoid documenting the change
options.rationale: Scheduling a window does not eliminate documentation requirements.

options.text: To bypass the approval process
options.rationale: A maintenance window is about timing, not skipping approvals.

stem: Which action is LEAST acceptable when handling an emergency change?

options.text: Skipping all documentation and the post-implementation review because it was urgent
options.rationale: Emergencies expedite approval but never authorize skipping documentation or the after-the-fact review, so this is least acceptable.

options.text: Obtaining expedited approval from the ECAB or emergency approver
options.rationale: Expedited approval is the correct emergency path, not an unacceptable action.

options.text: Confirming a rollback point before applying the fix
options.rationale: Ensuring rollback readiness is proper practice even in emergencies.

options.text: Performing a post-implementation review after the fix
options.rationale: A PIR after an emergency change is required good practice, not unacceptable.

stem: A deployed change causes unexpected failures in production. What capability BEST allows the team to restore service quickly?

options.text: Executing the predefined rollback (back-out) plan to the prior known-good state
options.rationale: A prepared rollback plan lets the team revert to the last stable state promptly when a change fails.

options.text: Improvising a fix with no prior plan
options.rationale: Improvising without a plan is slow and error-prone compared to a predefined rollback.

options.text: Deleting the change record
options.rationale: Deleting records does not restore service and harms accountability.

options.text: Waiting until the next maintenance window
options.rationale: Waiting prolongs the outage when an immediate rollback is available.

stem: What is the primary role of a Change Advisory Board (CAB)?

options.text: To review, prioritize, and approve or reject proposed changes based on risk and impact
options.rationale: The CAB is a cross-functional governance body that evaluates and authorizes changes.

options.text: To personally implement every production change
options.rationale: The CAB governs changes; it does not perform the technical implementation.

options.text: To write all software for the organization
options.rationale: Development is not the CAB's function.

options.text: To manage employee payroll
options.rationale: Payroll is unrelated to the CAB's change-governance role.

stem: Which statement MOST accurately describes what 'emergency' compresses in the emergency change process?

options.text: It compresses the approval timeline but not the requirements for documentation, rollback, and post-review
options.rationale: Emergency changes speed up authorization only; records, rollback readiness, and the PIR are still required.

options.text: It removes the need for any approval or record
options.rationale: Emergencies still require expedited approval and documentation; nothing eliminates them.

options.text: It allows permanent unapproved production access
options.rationale: Emergency change does not grant standing unapproved access.

options.text: It eliminates the rollback plan requirement
options.rationale: A rollback plan is still expected before applying an emergency change.

stem: A moderate-risk change with uncertain impact needs assessment before it is allowed. Which change category BEST fits, and what does it require?

options.text: A normal change requiring full CAB review and approval
options.rationale: Moderate-to-high risk changes needing assessment go through the full CAB process as normal changes.

options.text: A standard change needing no review
options.rationale: Standard changes are pre-approved and low-risk; an uncertain, moderate-risk change does not qualify.

options.text: An emergency change bypassing assessment
options.rationale: There is no emergency described, so the expedited emergency path is inappropriate.

options.text: An unapproved change requiring nothing
options.rationale: No legitimate change is 'unapproved requiring nothing'; controls always apply.

stem: A reviewer rejects an RFC because it omits one critical element that would allow safe reversal if the change fails. Which missing element is MOST likely the cause?

options.text: The rollback (back-out) plan
options.rationale: An RFC lacking a rollback plan is not ready, since there would be no defined way to revert a failed change.

options.text: The color of the change ticket
options.rationale: Ticket color is irrelevant to change readiness.

options.text: The lunch schedule of the implementers
options.rationale: This is unrelated to safe reversal of a change.

options.text: A marketing plan for the change
options.rationale: Marketing is not a change-readiness element for reversal.

stem: An auditor wants to know which process ensures every production modification is reviewed and authorized before it happens. This is MOST directly the responsibility of which process?

options.text: Change management
options.rationale: Reviewing and authorizing modifications before they occur is the defining function of change management.

options.text: Configuration management
options.rationale: Configuration management maintains the baseline of deployed state; it does not itself authorize each modification.

options.text: Incident management
options.rationale: Incident management responds to adverse events, not the pre-authorization of planned changes.

options.text: Capacity management
options.rationale: Capacity management plans resources; it does not authorize production changes.

stem: From a security standpoint, what is a PRIMARY reason change management insists every change be reversible and traceable?

options.text: So a failed or harmful change can be undone and every change can be attributed and audited
options.rationale: Reversibility limits the impact of bad changes, and traceability supports accountability and auditing.

options.text: So changes can be hidden from auditors
options.rationale: Traceability supports auditing rather than hiding changes.

options.text: So no one is ever accountable for changes
options.rationale: Traceability increases accountability, not the reverse.

options.text: So changes can be made without any record
options.rationale: Change management requires records; recordless changes defeat its purpose.

stem: The full CAB cannot convene in time to authorize an urgent fix. Which body is BEST suited to provide rapid authorization?

options.text: The Emergency Change Advisory Board (ECAB)
options.rationale: The ECAB is a reduced-quorum subset of the CAB that can rapidly authorize emergency changes.

options.text: The full marketing department
options.rationale: Marketing has no role in authorizing emergency technical changes.

options.text: No one; the change should proceed unapproved
options.rationale: Emergency changes still require expedited authorization, which the ECAB provides.

options.text: The external auditors
options.rationale: Auditors assess controls; they do not authorize operational emergency changes.

stem: After an emergency change is applied at night, when should the post-implementation review occur?

options.text: After the fact, as part of documenting and reviewing the emergency change
options.rationale: Emergency changes still receive a PIR after the fact to confirm results and capture lessons learned.

options.text: Never, because emergencies are exempt from review
options.rationale: Emergencies are not exempt; the PIR is still required.

options.text: Only if the change failed
options.rationale: A PIR is performed regardless of success to confirm outcomes and capture improvements.

options.text: Before the change is applied
options.rationale: A post-implementation review, by definition, occurs after implementation.

stem: Why does CISSP treat change management as an operational security control rather than merely an IT convenience?

options.text: Because uncontrolled changes are a leading cause of outages and can introduce vulnerabilities or break controls
options.rationale: Governing changes prevents modifications that reduce availability, weaken controls, or add vulnerabilities, making it a security control.

options.text: Because it speeds up changes by removing all oversight
options.rationale: Change management adds disciplined oversight; it does not remove it.

options.text: Because it eliminates the need for any testing
options.rationale: Change management includes testing; it does not eliminate it.

options.text: Because it guarantees no change will ever fail
options.rationale: It reduces and manages risk but cannot guarantee zero failures, which is why rollback exists.
